# Public procurement as a demand engine for circular and sustainable food value chains

## Scope and evidence status

This is a bounded evidence base, not an essay. I have prioritised primary law, official guidance, official statistics, municipal reports and project reports with direct operational data. I distinguish **fact**, **inference**, **secondary mention**, **not found** and **contradicted** explicitly. I also separate **EU procurement law**, **Danish practice**, and **Norwegian legal basis**. The main bottom line is that Copenhagen is a strong **benchmark on mechanism**, but **not a Norwegian template by default**: the evidence points to a mix of procurement design, kitchen conversion, menu redesign, seasonal planning, food-waste reduction, reporting and funded advisory support, rather than procurement clauses alone. citeturn20view0turn22view0turn21search5turn25view0turn26view1

**Legend used below**

| label | meaning |
|---|---|
| fact | directly supported by primary or near-primary source |
| inference | synthesis across sources; stated as inference |
| secondary mention | useful context, but not primary |
| not found | I did not locate a primary source confirming it |
| contradicted | source base points the other way |
| deckklart internt | good enough for internal deck use |
| needs-primary-check | usable, but should be validated against a stronger primary source |
| needs-data | gap remains |
| benchmark-only | useful benchmark, limited direct transferability |

## Regulatory table

| topic | legal basis | what is allowed | what is not allowed / caveat | evidence class | Norway transfer note | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equal treatment and non-discrimination | EU Directive 2014/24/EU Article 18; Norwegian anskaffelsesloven § 4 | Buyers may pursue sustainability, but must treat suppliers equally, without discrimination, and act proportionately. citeturn28search16turn28search0turn44search1turn26view2 | A tender cannot be designed to favour domestic or local suppliers as such. That means “local”, “Norwegian”, or geographic-origin requirements are not safe as stand-alone eligibility or award conditions. citeturn28search12turn25view0turn25view3 | fact | This is the core Norwegian legal constraint on “local food” procurement. | deckklart internt |
| Sustainability requirements in technical specifications | EU Directive 2014/24/EU Article 42 | Technical specifications may refer to characteristics and to a specific process or method of production or another life-cycle stage, provided they are linked to the subject matter of the contract. That creates legal room for organic production methods, animal-welfare characteristics, lower-impact production requirements and similar food attributes. citeturn27search2turn10search0turn27search23 | Unless justified by the subject matter, technical specifications must not refer to a specific make, source or origin. citeturn27search0turn27search13 | fact | In Norway, this is implemented through FOA rules on specifications and interpreted through DFØ guidance. | deckklart internt |
| Organic and other sustainability labels | EU Directive 2014/24/EU Article 43; FOA § 15-3; DFØ label guidance | Buyers may require a particular label, or use it as documentation for specific environmental or social characteristics, in the specification, award criteria or contract conditions, provided equivalent labels or equivalent documentation are accepted. citeturn27search1turn44search0turn25view2 | Buyers cannot require a private or discriminatory label without allowing equivalents. citeturn25view2turn25view3 | fact | Organic certification is legally usable in Norwegian food procurement, but it must be framed as label-or-equivalent. | deckklart internt |
| Award criteria for sustainability | EU Directive 2014/24/EU Article 67 | Contracts can be awarded on best price-quality ratio using environmental and social aspects linked to the contract subject matter. That supports climate footprint, menu composition, animal welfare and similar food-service performance criteria. citeturn27search17turn10search5 | Criteria still need to be linked to the contract subject matter and be assessable in a transparent way. citeturn27search21turn26view2 | fact | Norwegian rules add a climate/environment minimum-weighting regime. | deckklart internt |
| Contract performance clauses | EU Directive 2014/24/EU Article 70 | Buyers may set special performance conditions relating to environmental or social considerations, if linked to the contract and stated in procurement documents. That is a route for food-waste reporting, delivery routines, packaging, staff training, or menu-performance follow-up. citeturn27search11turn27search8 | Cannot use contract clauses to backdoor origin discrimination. | fact | Transferable to Norwegian food-service and catering contracts. | deckklart internt |
| Local food in Norway | DFØ guidance on “Lokalprodusert mat” | DFØ states that buyers **cannot** require local production or Norwegian production, but **can** describe wanted product characteristics, ask for products in Norwegian season, and split procurements so smaller suppliers can bid. citeturn25view0 | “Local” or “produced in Norway” as a direct requirement is not allowed. citeturn25view0 | fact | This is the clearest Norwegian practice guidance for transferability. | deckklart internt |
| Seasonal requirements in Norway | DFØ guidance; DFØ sample catering criteria | DFØ explicitly says buyers may ask for products in Norwegian season. DFØ sample criteria for catering also show a practical formulation requiring at least 50% fresh ingredients in season. citeturn25view0turn24search15 | This is guidance and sample text, not court-tested black-letter law. Use with subject-matter linkage and proportionality. | fact | Stronger than “local”, safer when framed as product/menu characteristic. | deckklart internt |
| Climate and environment as mandatory consideration in Norway | anskaffelsesloven § 5; FOA § 7-9; DFØ guidance | Public buyers shall organise procurement to reduce harmful environmental impact and promote climate-friendly solutions where relevant; under current FOA § 7-9, buyers must weight climate/environment at minimum 30%, or replace weighting with requirements in the specification if that clearly gives better effect and is justified. citeturn45search16turn26view1 | There is an exception where impacts are insignificant and justified. Also, the wider 2026 law reform mostly enters into force from 1 July 2026, so legal citations should distinguish current FOA from forthcoming changes. citeturn46search0turn46search2 | fact | This is the main Norwegian home rule for sustainability leverage in food procurement right now. | deckklart internt |
| EU-level seasonal criterion | JRC technical work on EU GPP food criteria | The EU food-criteria revision notes that an explicit “seasonal produce” criterion was removed from the food procurement criteria set because seasonality captures only one dimension and can slide toward production-place issues. citeturn30search1turn30search4 | This is **not** a ban on seasonal menus. It is a caution about criterion design. | fact + inference | Norway can still use seasonality, but must frame it carefully as a product/menu/time-of-year characteristic rather than an origin proxy. | deckklart internt |
| “Local food requirements are lawful if motivated by sustainability” | No supporting primary source found; DFØ says the opposite | None. | This claim is **contradicted** by DFØ’s guidance and by EU/Norwegian equal-treatment rules. citeturn25view0turn28search16turn44search1 | contradicted | Do not use this framing in a Norwegian transfer memo. | deckklart internt |

| “Copenhagen did it with no added public spending” | contradicted in strong form | contradicted | JRC cites kitchen-budget-neutral conversion, but municipal reports show dedicated food-quality and development funding. citeturn21search5turn22view0 | deckklart internt |

## Barrier table

| barrier class | source-backed observation | evidence class | relevance for Norway transfer | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market volume | In Viken’s value-chain study, suppliers state that higher organic production requires buyers to commit to sufficient volume; without predictable demand, producers are reluctant to invest or expand. citeturn37view1turn37view3turn37view0 | fact | This is the single most repeated bottleneck in the Norwegian material. Public demand helps only if it is stable and credible over time. | deckklart internt |
| Distribution and availability | Viken canteens experienced catalogue items that were not actually in stock, substitution problems, and fragile supply where one supplier failure caused weeks without organic eggs. citeturn37view1turn36view4 | fact | Indicates that procurement ambition must be matched by logistics/data integration and backup supply design. | deckklart internt |
| Price | The AgriAnalyse/Landbruksdirektoratet-backed Viken study identifies price pressure and budget limits as major obstacles; in one supplier example, organic dairy products averaged around 30% higher than conventional. citeturn36view2turn37view3 | fact | If Norway leans only on tender weighting and not menu redesign, cost pressure will likely dominate. | deckklart internt |
| Regulation | Norwegian guidance says local or Norwegian origin cannot be required directly. That constrains “kortreist” ambitions and pushes buyers toward legal proxies: season, animal welfare, product characteristics, lotting and dynamic assortment. citeturn25view0turn25view3 | fact | This is a legal design barrier, not a policy impossibility. | deckklart internt |
| Kitchen capacity and competence | Copenhagen’s model relied on advisory tracks, workshops, recipe banks and capability building; Viken’s model explicitly links procurement with food-professional competence and simpler from-scratch concepts. citeturn22view0turn33view0turn21search5 | fact | Transfer requires capacity-building budgets and implementation support, not just tender clauses. | deckklart internt |
| Data and monitoring | Copenhagen uses regular organic/climate reporting; Viken built quarterly purchase analyses; Oslo’s action plan explicitly calls for digital waste-measurement and reporting tools. At the same time, a current Oslo-wide organic-share figure was not located, and national Norwegian public-meal share statistics were not located. citeturn6view6turn34view5turn14search0turn42view0 | fact | Data maturity is uneven; this weakens benchmarking and follow-up in Norway. | deckklart internt |

Too-static catalogues and weak agreement management create friction. citeturn37view2turn36view4 | fact | High relevance: transferability depends on framework-agreement architecture, not only political targets. | deckklart internt |

## Short judgement

The strongest **lawful** demand-side levers for Norway are not “buy local” clauses. They are: **label-or-equivalent organic requirements; subject-matter-linked production/process requirements; seasonal and menu-performance requirements; food-waste and climate reporting; lotting and dynamic assortment; and implementation support for kitchens**. That mix is clearly visible in both Copenhagen and the stronger Norwegian practice material. citeturn25view0turn25view2turn26view1turn22view0turn33view0

Copenhagen’s benchmark value is real, but its transfer lesson is **mechanism**, not just **result**. The municipal evidence does **not** support the claim that Copenhagen got to a very high organic share through procurement requirements alone, nor that it did so without public implementation support. citeturn22view0turn21search5turn5view2turn6view6

For Norway, the evidence base is materially weaker on **measured public-meal shares** than on **policy intent** and **pilot implementation**. Oslo’s citywide current organic-share figure for all public meals was not located in a primary source, and a national official time series for public-meal organic share was also not located. That means any Norway-vs-Copenhagen slide should carry a clear **data-gap caveat**. citeturn13view0turn13view1turn42view0

### Do not say

- “EU/EØS procurement law lets Norwegian public buyers require local food.”
- “Copenhagen proved that procurement specifications alone can deliver a 90% organic share.”
- “Oslo currently has a verified citywide organic share for public meals of X%.”  
- “Danish municipal practice can be copied directly into Norwegian tenders without legal adaptation.”
- “Seasonal is just a lawful proxy for local.”  
- “Higher organic share necessarily means higher procurement budgets.”
